Sixth grade science · Unit 3

Forces, Motion & Energy

Why does a roller coaster go fastest at the bottom of a hill? Why is a full shopping cart so hard to stop? Why does an egg survive a fall onto a pillow but not onto the floor? Every motion you see comes from forces and energy, and both follow rules you can calculate.

Where we left off: Unit 2 showed that thermal energy is particles jiggling, and that energy moves from hot to cold. Here we use the same energy ideas for moving objects, and we will see that friction is one way motion turns into heat.

Concept 1 · Describing motion

Speed is distance per time

Speed tells you how far something goes in each second: speed = distance ÷ time. On a distance–time graph, a steeper line means faster.

Analogy

Two delivery drivers

Both drivers cover the same 10 miles. Driver A arrives in 10 minutes; Driver B takes 20. Same distance, less time means a higher speed. Speed = distance ÷ time, so A averages 1 mile per minute (60 mph) and B averages 0.5 (30 mph).

Where it breaks: a real car speeds up, stops at lights, and slows in traffic. Average speed hides all of that; a distance–time graph shows it.

Try it

Race on a 150 m track

Data

Distance–time graph

Slope = rise ÷ run = distance ÷ time = speed. A flat line means standing still. Move the time slider above and watch the dots slide along each line.

Concept 2 · What changes motion

Balanced and unbalanced forces

A force is a push or a pull. If forces are balanced, motion doesn't change. If they're unbalanced, the object speeds up, slows down, or turns. A bigger net force or a smaller mass means more acceleration. Mass also measures inertia: how hard something is to start moving or to stop. A full cart is harder to get going and harder to stop.

Analogy

Tug of war

In a tug of war, each team pulls the rope with a force, measured in newtons (N). A force has a size and a direction, so you can add forces up. Pulls in opposite directions subtract: net force = bigger pull − smaller pull, pointing toward the stronger team.

If both teams pull with 300 N, the net force is 0 N. The forces are balanced, so the rope's motion does not change. Add a fourth kid on one side and the net force is 100 N toward that team. The forces are now unbalanced, and the rope starts to speed up that way.

Where it breaks: balanced does not always mean standing still. A rope already moving at a steady speed also has balanced forces. Balanced just means the motion is not changing.

Try it

Pull the cart

Data

Same push, different masses: acceleration

a = F ÷ m. Doubling the force doubles the acceleration. Doubling the mass halves it. The dots show your current cart and net force from the sliders above.

Concept 3 · Two forces you always meet

Friction and gravity

Sliding friction pushes against sliding between surfaces. Gravity pulls everything toward the center of Earth. Together they explain why things stop and why things fall. Friction can also help things move: it is what lets your shoes grip the floor when you walk and your tires grip the road.

Analogy

Dragging your feet on a hike

Drag your feet along a dirt path and you feel something grab them. That grab is friction. Even a floor that feels smooth is jagged up close: under a strong microscope it looks like a mountain range of tiny peaks and valleys. Press two surfaces together and their peaks and valleys lock into each other. To slide, you have to push the peaks past each other, and that snagging pushes against the motion.

The snagging also makes the tiny bumps shake. Shaking particles are thermal energy (Unit 2), which is why rubbing your hands together makes them warm.

Where it breaks: the real picture is more than bumps. Surfaces also stick to each other a little at the atomic level. Friction happens between every pair of surfaces that touch and slide, and you cannot turn it off.

Diagram

All the forces on a sliding book

Start with something you know. Put a textbook on a desk and give it a shove. It slides a little way, then stops. While it slides, three forces act on the book: gravity pulls it down, the table pushes it up, and friction drags it backward. The picture shows all three.

Up and down cancel, so the book doesn't sink or float. Nothing pushes forward to balance friction, so the book slows down.

Try it

Slide a sled across different surfaces

Data

How far does it slide?

Sliding distance = speed² ÷ (2 × friction coefficient × 9.8). Starting speed 6 m/s. Less friction means a much longer slide. Rounded textbook coefficients.

Concept 4 · Two kinds of energy

Stored and moving

Potential energy is stored energy (height makes gravitational potential energy). Kinetic energy is energy of motion. A roller coaster trades one for the other all ride long.

Diagram

Stored energy and moving energy

Potential energy is stored energy that is waiting to be used. A ball at the top of a hill has it, and so do a stretched rubber band and a book on a high shelf. The higher up (or the more stretched), the more is stored.

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: a rolling ball, a runner, a falling book. The faster it moves, and the more mass it has, the more kinetic energy it has. As the ball rolls downhill, its stored energy turns into moving energy.

Roller coaster lab

Move the car along the track, or press Ride it. The bars and the chart below show how stored and moving energy trade places.

Concept 5 · Where energy goes

Energy changes form

When energy changes form, some of it always ends up as thermal energy (heat) and sound that we cannot easily use.

Analogy

A leaky bucket

The leaks are the energy you did not want to lose. Where does it go? Mostly into heat. When surfaces rub, the bumps snag and the particles in both surfaces start to shake more, and shaking particles are thermal energy. When a ball thuds on the floor, the ball and the floor both warm up a tiny bit. Sound is tiny shakes of the air that spread out and fade, and in the end they warm the air a tiny bit too.

The water that leaked did not disappear. It went somewhere you did not want it. Wasted energy is still energy, and usually it is heat.

Try it

Drop different balls

Data

Bounce heights shrink

Each bounce keeps a fixed fraction of the energy. The missing energy went to heat (the ball and floor warm up a tiny bit) and sound (the thud).

Diagram

Where does the energy go?

Rounded teaching values. LED bulbs turn a much bigger share into light, which is why they run cooler and cost less to power. A gasoline car typically turns only about 12 to 30 of every 100 J of fuel into motion, while an electric car turns roughly 87 of every 100 J of battery energy into motion (U.S. Department of Energy). Muscles turn about a quarter of the food energy they use into motion.

Real world

A refrigerator does not make cold, it moves heat

A refrigerator uses electricity to pump heat out of the food box and release it into your kitchen. That is why the coils on the back feel warm. The less heat leaks in through the walls and door, and the better the pump, the less electricity it needs.

RefrigeratorElectricity it uses
Typical new refrigerator sold in 2001baseline (100%)
New ENERGY STAR refrigeratorabout 40% less than that baseline (U.S. Department of Energy)

Over a refrigerator's 10 or more years running day and night, that difference is a lot of energy, and a lot less heat dumped into the air.

Real world

Concept 6 · When things collide

Equal pushes, softer stops

When two things collide, they push on each other with equal and opposite forces. That's Newton's third law. You can't make the force go away, but you can make it smaller by stretching the stop over more time.

Analogy

Catching a water balloon

The balloon has to lose all its speed either way. Losing it slowly takes a gentle push; losing it all at once takes a huge one.

Diagram

Car meets truck

The pushes are exactly equal. The car's motion changes nine times more because it has less mass, so less inertia. That's why the people in the small car get jolted hardest.

Try it

Drop an egg from 1 meter

Data

Longer stop, smaller force

Every egg hits at the same speed, about 4.4 m/s. Softer surfaces stretch the stop out, so the push is smaller. Rounded teaching values; a real egg cracks somewhere around 25 N.

Build it

Engineering challenge: the egg lander

The problem: design something that lets a raw egg survive a drop from 2 meters (about the height of a top bunk).

Your materials: up to 10 sheets of paper, 1 meter of masking tape, and 10 straws. Nothing else. The egg must come out so you can check it.

  1. Plan. Sketch two different ideas. For each one, write one sentence on how it makes the egg's stop take longer.
  2. Build the idea you think is better.
  3. Test from 1 meter first, then 2 meters. Write down what happened each time.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it. Real engineers repeat this loop many times.

Tie-breaker: if two landers both work, the lighter one wins. Drop over a trash bag. Print a design log for each team.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Why is a roller coaster fastest at the bottom of the first hill, and why can't the second hill be taller than the first?

Show a model answer

At the top of the first hill the car has lots of stored (potential) energy. Rolling down turns it into moving (kinetic) energy, so speed is highest at the bottom.

Energy can't be created. Friction and air resistance even take some away as heat. So the car can never climb higher than where it started.

0 of 9 correct

Words to know

speed
Distance traveled per unit time.
force
A push or a pull, measured in newtons.
net force
All forces on an object added together.
balanced
Forces cancel; motion doesn't change.
acceleration
How quickly speed or direction changes.
inertia
How much an object resists a change in its motion. More mass means more inertia.
friction
Force between touching surfaces that opposes sliding.
gravity
Pull between objects with mass; on Earth, it pulls things down.
potential energy
Stored energy, such as from height or stretch.
kinetic energy
Energy of motion.
energy transformation
Energy changing from one form to another, like stored energy becoming moving energy.
Newton's third law
When two objects push on each other, the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): a toy car or marble, a ramp (board and books), tape measure, stopwatch (phone), spring scale or rubber band, sandpaper, wax paper, a few balls, a skateboard-like toy, raw eggs, paper, masking tape, and straws for the egg lander.

  • Concept 1: mark a 5 m line, time a classmate's walk, jog, and hop, then compute speeds.
  • Concept 2: stretch a rubber band tied to a loaded vs empty cart and compare stretch to acceleration.
  • Concept 3: slide the same block down a ramp lined with sandpaper, plain board, and wax paper.
  • Concept 4: release a marble from different ramp heights and measure how far it launches a cup.
  • Concept 5: drop different balls from 1 m and photograph the bounce height next to a meter stick.
  • Concept 6: the egg lander challenge (one longer session). Push two rolling carts or skateboards together to feel equal and opposite pushes.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Moving things need a continuing force." Without friction, motion would continue by itself.
  • "Heavier things fall faster." In air without much drag, they fall at the same rate.
  • "Energy gets used up." It changes form; some becomes heat.
  • "No motion means no forces." Balanced forces can be present.
  • "In a crash, the bigger object pushes harder." The forces are equal; the smaller object's motion changes more.
  • "Padding makes the force go away." It makes the force smaller by making the stop take longer.

Pacing: about six 30-minute sessions, plus one longer session for the egg lander.
